sections.h: Chapters 13-20: sign-acts, drought and the confessions
sections.b: These chapters hold four of Jeremiah's sign-acts (the loincloth, the celibate life, the potter's house, the broken jar), the drought liturgy of chapter 14 and the middle of his confessions: 15:10-21, 17:12-18, 18:18-23 and 20:7-18. They show a man whose life and words are one message and who argues with God about the cost. The conflict with Pashhur (20:1-6) is the first open persecution in the book, and Babylon is first named as the enemy there (20:4).
sections.refs: Jeremiah 13:1-11; Jeremiah 15:10-21; Jeremiah 16:1-9; Jeremiah 18:1-6; Jeremiah 19:1-15; Jeremiah 20:1-18

sections.b: Jeremiah acts out his messages: a buried loincloth, a childless life, a visit to a potter, a smashed jar. He also states a rule about prophecy itself: when the LORD threatens or promises a nation, the result depends on how the nation responds (Jeremiah 18:7-10). The same idea is behind Jonah. It means a prophecy of judgment is not a prediction that cannot change; it is an offer that can be taken up.

sections.h: The prophets who were not sent
sections.b: In Jeremiah 14:13-16 the LORD says the prophets who promise peace and food in the drought were never sent. Their messages are 'a false vision, divination, a worthless idol, and the deceit of their own hearts'. The test is the sending, the content and the outcome. Deuteronomy 18:20-22 is the background; Jeremiah 23 and 28 come back to it.

Moses and Samuel were the great intercessors. Jeremiah prays (Jeremiah 14:7-9, 19-22) and is then told three times not to (7:16; 11:14; 14:11), and in 15:1 that even Moses and Samuel would not move the LORD. The ban does not say prayer is wrong; it says the sentence is fixed.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 14:7-9; Jeremiah 14:11; Jeremiah 15:1; Exodus 32:11-14; 1 Samuel 12:19-23; Jeremiah 18:20

sections.b: Chapter 14 has the shape of a communal lament in time of drought. The confessions of 15:10-18, 17:12-18, 18:18-23 and 20:7-18 are laments of one man: complaint, a cry for revenge, a statement of trust. Unlike the Psalms they are tied to a particular life, and the LORD answers at times with a call to repent (15:19). The last of them, a curse on the day of birth (20:14-18), is parallel to Job 3.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 14:1-22; Jeremiah 15:10-18; Jeremiah 17:12-18; Jeremiah 18:18-23; Jeremiah 20:7-18; Job 3:1-26

sections.h: Turn back and be turned back
sections.b: The verb shuv, 'turn', is Jeremiah's key word. The people's 'turnings away' are many (14:7); Jeremiah himself is told 'If you turn back, I will turn you back' (15:19); the whole people are told to turn from their evil way, and answer that it is no use (18:11-12). The potter's rule (18:7-10) says that if a nation turns, the LORD relents.

sections.h: The sabbath sermon at the gates
sections.b: Jeremiah 17:19-27 is one of the longest sabbath texts outside the Torah. The people are to carry no loads through the city gates and do no work on the sabbath; if they keep it, the dynasty and city will last, and if not, fire will burn the fortresses of Jerusalem. Nehemiah applied it in his day (Nehemiah 13:15-22). The rabbis later counted carrying among the thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2).

sections.h: The valley of Ben-hinnom in Jeremiah
sections.b: Jeremiah 19 is set in the Valley of Ben-hinnom at the Potsherd Gate, where children had been burned at the Topheth. The LORD says it will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter and that the city will be made like Topheth. The later name Gehenna for the place of punishment comes from this valley.

Jeremiah 19:5 says the people built the high places of Baal to burn their sons in the fire, and the LORD says he never ordered it. Jeremiah 32:35 names Molech. The practice is forbidden in Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2-5, and Josiah defiled the Topheth (2 Kings 23:10).

sections.h: The LORD changes his mind (Jeremiah 15 and 18)
sections.b: In Jeremiah 18:7-10 the LORD says he will 'change his mind' about a planned harm if the nation turns, and of a promised good if the nation does evil. In 15:6 he says he is tired of relenting. These texts sit beside Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29, which say God does not change his mind. Church teachers have read the two sets together in different ways.

Jeremiah's confessions show a faithful man who suffers for his message and tells God so. In 15:18 he accuses the LORD of being a stream that fails; in 20:7 he says the LORD enticed him and won; in 20:14-18 he curses the day of his birth. The book records these as prayers, and the LORD answers not with an explanation but with a call to go on.

sections.h: The potter and the clay in Jeremiah 18
sections.b: The LORD tells Jeremiah that Israel is in his hand as clay in the potter's (Jeremiah 18:6). The next verses make the picture conditional: a nation's fate depends on its response (18:7-10). Paul uses the potter and clay picture in Romans 9:20-21, probably from Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9. Reformed and Methodist readers argue over whether Jeremiah 18 supports or limits a doctrine of unconditional election.

Jeremiah 17:1 says Judah's sin is cut into its heart with an iron pen; 17:9 says the heart is crooked and sick beyond healing, and asks who can know it. The KJV's 'desperately wicked' goes beyond the Hebrew. Churches have used the verse in the doctrine of original sin in different ways.

Jeremiah is told to hide a linen loincloth at Perath. Perath is the usual Hebrew name for the Euphrates (Genesis 2:14), though some think a nearer place, Parah (Joshua 18:23), is meant. The Euphrates is the river of Babylon, to which Judah would go into exile.

Jeremiah 16:2 forbids the prophet to take a wife or have children in this place, as a sign of the coming disaster. It is not a rule for others. The New Testament's reasons for celibacy are different (Matthew 19:12; 1 Corinthians 7:26-29).

In the order of the book, the LORD first names Babylon as the destroyer in Jeremiah 20:4, in his word against Pashhur: he will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon, who will carry them off and strike them down with the sword.
Jeremiah 16:4-6 says the dead of the land will lie unburied like dung, with no mourners and no cup of comfort. An unburied body was among the worst fates (Deuteronomy 28:26).
